answer.rationale: The competitive shock is a price attack on SMB, and the obvious reflex is promotional_pricing. Memory_73 explicitly records that promotional pricing does lift acquisition and revenue but materially damaged 30-day retention, with an explicit warning not to generalize it as a growth strategy. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, matching a deeper price cut would likely buy short-term retention of exactly the least durable accounts while degrading the revenue base — the wrong trade for this objective. Referral incentives (memory_57) are the only direction on record that added qualified revenue with no measurable harm to retention, so it is the best risk-adjusted lever for defending revenue quality under a price attack; it also works through established customers, which are the segment least likely to be poached on price alone. Caveats I am carrying rather than resolving: memory_57 was established in established customers, not in the price-sensitive SMB cohort that is actually churning, and it was not observed under competitive-shock conditions — so its transfer to this situation is an assumption, not a verified finding. I am therefore running this as a standard experiment with a retention and qualified-revenue holdout rather than a broad rollout, so the transfer assumption gets tested cheaply. Onboarding (memory_86, exp_86, clean +3% retention) and signup simplification (memory_31, exp_31, SMB-confirmed but retention -1% and not replicated off-SMB) remain sound background investments but are top-of-funnel and too slow to answer a churn spike this week. Enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is sound but addresses a different segment than the one under attack. Verification budget is spent, so no archive requests are issued; if budget reopens next week the priority checks are whether memory_57 holds in price-sensitive SMB and whether memory_73's retention damage was segment-specific or general.
